# Extreme Cold Grips Upper Midwest, Claims Life

(CNN) -- A brutal combination of frigid air and harsh winds slammed portions of the upper Midwest on Tuesday, subjecting several states to their harshest weather conditions in decades. A punishing cold front continues to hammer the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region.

Following closely behind a blizzard that swept through the Northern Plains, thermometers in Minneapolis, Minnesota, plunged to negative 18 degrees Fahrenheit. Tragically, in Hayward, Wisconsin, a man known for sleepwalking lost his life after being exposed to the bitter cold, according to CNN affiliate KDLH-TV based in Duluth, Minnesota. His son reported him missing around noon that day, and officers discovered a trail of bare footprints stretching 190 feet from his residence.

Meanwhile, Minneapolis resident Tony Williams learned firsthand how dangerous the cold could be. After spending 45 minutes clearing snow without gloves in negative-17-degree conditions, he developed second-degree frostbite, CNN affiliate KARE-TV reported. Dr. Cheryl Adkinson, the emergency room physician at Hennepin County Medical Center who treated him, described blistering across his fingertips and thumb.

Grand Forks, North Dakota, shattered a decades-old temperature record dating to 1979, plummeting to negative 37 degrees, the National Weather Service reported.

## Widespread Disruption

The combination of frigid air, snowfall, and ice created chaos for commuters throughout the region. Numerous schools and businesses across the Midwest closed their doors, while residents worked to clear vehicles and roadways buried under snow and ice.

In Arlington Heights, Illinois, railway employee Matt Tesh experienced firsthand the danger of near-zero wind chills while clearing snow from train tracks Tuesday morning, according to CNN affiliate WGN. Despite bundling up in multiple layers beneath his safety coat, he attempted to work without face protection—a decision he quickly regretted. "Two or three minutes [without it], and my face was burning," he told the station.

## No Relief in Sight

Meteorologists warn that conditions won't improve significantly in coming days. A weather pattern called an "Alberta clipper" is forecast to bring strong winds, falling temperatures, and additional snow accumulation to Chicago by Wednesday morning, per weather service projections.

CNN meteorologist Guillermo Arduino explained that this Canadian-originated system would collide with an Arctic air mass, pushing subfreezing temperatures across the entire Great Lakes region. The convergence is expected to produce the season's coldest stretch yet for much of the Midwest, accompanied by dangerous wind chill values.

Forecasters anticipate snowfall totals ranging from 1 to 5 inches stretching from the Dakotas through the southern Great Lakes, potentially reaching the Northeast by week's end. The weather service's central region office warned that "near-whiteout conditions and slick roads are expected to impact travel of all types."

## Air Travel Continues to Suffer

Building on disruptions from earlier storms, airports serving Chicago, Minneapolis, Milwaukee, and both Grand Rapids and Detroit in Michigan are bracing for ongoing delays, according to Arduino.

Detroit's temperatures are projected to hit negative 18 degrees Wednesday, followed by negative 12 degrees Thursday. Minneapolis residents can expect even harsher conditions, with temperatures dropping to negative 21 degrees Wednesday and negative 29 degrees Thursday.

Bismarck, North Dakota, will see temperatures near negative 20 degrees Wednesday, with wind chills plunging to negative 45 degrees. The city may also receive an additional 3 to 6 inches of snow, adding to the 5 inches already deposited by the previous storm system.

A brutal cold front tore through the upper Midwest and Great Lakes region this week, subjecting millions of residents to some of the most extreme temperatures the area has experienced in decades. Combined with dangerous wind conditions, the frigid weather system has proven both disruptive and, in at least one tragic case, fatal.

## Minneapolis Buried Under Blizzard, Then Deep Freeze

Minneapolis, Minnesota bore the brunt of this weather system on two fronts. First, a powerful blizzard swept across the Northern Plains, blanketing the region in heavy snow. In the storm's aftermath, temperatures plummeted to a bone-chilling minus 18 degrees Fahrenheit, leaving residents to contend with both the snow's aftermath and the punishing cold that followed.

## A Tragic Loss in Hayward, Wisconsin

The extreme cold proved fatal for one Wisconsin man. In Hayward, an individual with a known history of sleepwalking wandered outside his home—reportedly traveling only about 190 feet—while barefoot and unprotected from the elements. Exposed to the dangerous cold without proper clothing, he succumbed to hypothermia, underscoring how quickly and quietly such extreme temperatures can turn deadly, even for those who venture only a short distance from safety.

## The Physical Toll of Winter Labor

The cold also took a physical toll on those who ventured outside to manage the aftermath of the storm. Schools and businesses across multiple states were forced to close their doors, as officials prioritized public safety over normal operations, urging residents to stay indoors and avoid unnecessary travel during the height of the cold snap.

# Arctic Blast Grips Upper Midwest, Blamed for at Least 7 Deaths as Temperatures Plunge to Historic Lows

**Minneapolis, Minnesota** — A dangerous arctic air mass has settled over the upper Midwest this week, bringing life-threatening wind chills, widespread travel disruptions, and at least seven confirmed deaths across the region, officials said Thursday.

Temperatures in Minneapolis-St. Paul dropped to -26°F Wednesday morning, with wind chills reaching as low as -50°F, according to the National Weather Service. Fargo, North Dakota, recorded a low of -31°F, while International Falls, Minnesota — often nicknamed the "Icebox of the Nation" — hit -37°F, nearing daily records for the date.

"We're looking at conditions where exposed skin can experience frostbite in under 10 minutes," said NWS meteorologist Karen Aldous. "This is not just cold — this is dangerous, life-threatening cold."

**Deaths Linked to Exposure and Accidents**

Authorities in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and the Dakotas say at least seven deaths have been attributed to the cold snap so far. Hennepin County officials confirmed two individuals experiencing homelessness died of suspected hypothermia in Minneapolis. In Wisconsin, a Milwaukee man was found dead in his unheated home Tuesday, and authorities in South Dakota reported a motorist died after becoming stranded in a snowdrift for several hours.

"We are urging everyone — especially vulnerable populations — to seek warming shelters immediately," said Minneapolis Mayor's office spokesperson Elena Vasquez. Cities across the region have opened emergency warming centers in libraries, community centers, and transit stations.

**Travel Chaos Across the Region**

The extreme cold has wreaked havoc on transportation. More than 400 flights were canceled at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport on Wednesday alone, with airlines citing concerns over ground equipment failures and de-icing complications in sub-zero temperatures.

Amtrak suspended service on portions of its Empire Builder route connecting Chicago to Seattle, citing frozen switches and signal equipment. Interstate 94 was closed for several hours Tuesday night near Fargo after a multi-vehicle pileup caused by whiteout conditions and black ice, injuring at least twelve people, according to North Dakota Highway Patrol.

School districts across Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, and South Dakota canceled classes for a second consecutive day, affecting hundreds of thousands of students.

**Strain on Infrastructure**

Utility companies have reported record-breaking demand as residents crank up heating systems. Xcel Energy, which serves much of Minnesota, asked customers to lower thermostats to 60 degrees during peak hours to prevent potential outages, warning that natural gas supplies were being strained by the prolonged cold.

"We've seen demand spike to levels we typically don't see until deeper into winter," said Xcel spokesperson Michael Chen. "We're asking for conservation not because supply is at immediate risk, but to maintain system stability."

**Relief in Sight, But Not Immediately**

Forecasters say the polar vortex responsible for the extreme temperatures is expected to begin retreating by the weekend, with highs climbing back into the teens and twenties by Sunday. Until then, the National Weather Service has extended wind chill warnings and advisories across an eight-state region stretching from Montana to Michigan.

"It will feel like a heat wave when we get back to single digits," Aldous said. "But we're not there yet, and people need to take this seriously for at least a few more days."

Officials continue to urge residents to check on elderly neighbors, avoid unnecessary travel, and ensure pets are brought indoors as the dangerous cold persists.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Alberta Clipper Brings Dangerous Wind Chills, Snow to Great Lakes Region

**CHICAGO (AP)** — A fast-moving winter storm system known as an "Alberta clipper" swept through the Great Lakes region Wednesday, bringing gusty snow squalls and plunging temperatures that pushed wind chills to dangerous levels across several states.

The clipper system, which originated in the Canadian province of Alberta before racing southeast across the northern Plains, dropped several inches of snow in parts of Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan before pushing into Illinois, Indiana and Ohio by midday.

The National Weather Service issued wind chill warnings and advisories for millions of residents, with forecasters warning that exposed skin could experience frostbite in as little as 15 minutes in the hardest-hit areas.

"These clipper systems move fast, but they pack a real punch when it comes to wind," said meteorologist Sarah Chen with the National Weather Service's Chicago office. "The snow itself isn't usually the main story with an Alberta clipper — it's the brutal cold that follows behind it, driven by strong winds out of the northwest."

Wind chills were expected to plummet to between 20 and 35 degrees below zero in parts of Minnesota, North Dakota and Wisconsin overnight into Thursday morning, with somewhat less severe but still dangerous conditions — 10 to 20 below zero — stretching into the Chicago metropolitan area, Detroit and Cleveland.

Officials in several cities opened warming centers for homeless residents and others without adequate heat. Chicago Mayor's office confirmed at least a dozen warming buses would be stationed near CTA stations overnight.

Schools in parts of Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula announced early dismissals or delayed openings Thursday, citing concerns about children waiting at bus stops in extreme cold.

Air travel also felt the effects, with more than 400 flights canceled at Chicago's O'Hare and Midway airports by Wednesday evening, according to tracking service FlightAware. Airlines cited both the snow squalls, which reduced visibility along Lake Michigan, and ground crew safety concerns in the extreme cold.

The Michigan State Police reported multiple crashes on Interstate 94 near Kalamazoo attributed to sudden whiteout conditions from lake-effect snow bands enhanced by the clipper's passage. No fatalities were immediately reported, though several injuries were confirmed.

"Visibility went from a mile to essentially zero in about two minutes," said Sgt. David Torres. "We're urging people to avoid unnecessary travel until this system clears the region."

Lake-effect snow warnings remained in effect for areas downwind of Lakes Superior, Michigan and Erie, where localized totals could reach 6 to 12 inches through Thursday as cold air moving over the relatively warmer lake waters generates additional snow bands.

Forecasters said the clipper system would continue pushing eastward overnight, bringing similar conditions to Pennsylvania, upstate New York and New England by Thursday and Friday before finally clearing the Northeast by the weekend.

Despite the storm's swift movement — a hallmark of Alberta clippers, which typically pass through a region in under 24 hours — officials cautioned that the cold air mass settling in behind it would linger for several days.

"The snow will move out fairly quickly," Chen said. "But everyone needs to prepare for a stretch of genuinely dangerous cold that follows. This isn't just uncomfortable weather — this is the kind of cold that can be life-threatening if people aren't careful."

Residents were urged to check on elderly neighbors, bring pets indoors, and ensure vehicles have emergency supplies including blankets and phone chargers in case of travel delays.

The weather service advised residents across the affected region to limit time outdoors, dress in layers, and keep extremities covered through the end of the week as arctic air continues to dominate the pattern.
